title: Eval tiered guardrails for low-cost variants (WIP)
summary: Working notes on a lightweight, tiered quality-guardrail approach to enable use of lower-cost model/quantization configurations while bounding user-visible regressions. Includes proposed thresholds, measurement slices, spreadsheet knobs, rollout checklist, and outstanding tradeoffs.
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a proposed operational pattern for allowing cheaper model configurations (smaller model variants, higher quantization, mixed precision) to be used in production under strict, automated quality gates. The goal is to materially reduce per-token cost for eligible traffic while limiting customer-facing regressions and keeping eval overhead (and eval $) bounded.

Background / why this matters:
- Hosting cost pressure: for many customers, 10–30% unit-cost savings unlocks sizable margin improvements or allows more generous rate limits.
- Current problem: we have good single-config rollouts (A/B/canary) but lack a low-friction, automated guardrail system for broad use of cheaper configs across routes. Manual evals are slow and expensive.
- Desired: a repeatable, spreadsheet-driven decision process + runtime enforcement that ties cheaper-config eligibility to measured eval pass-rates and an adjustable regression budget.

High-level design (tiered guardrail):
1) Candidate selection: define a cheaper variant (e.g., Llama-2-13B -> quantized 4-bit + kernel optimizations) per model family and per workload class.
2) Per-route eval slices: for each API route we maintain 4–6 evaluation slices (e.g., instruction-following, safety, long-context, entity recall, numeric precision). These live in the eval suite spreadsheet.
3) Quality gates: each slice has a threshold (pass% or metric delta). The cheaper variant must pass all critical slices and have aggregate regression <= regression_budget (see below).
4) Regression budget: a soft budget expressed as an expected cost-of-quality (COQ) cap — i.e., expected 1W of additional human review or rollback cost translated into dollars.
5) Auto-enforcement: if cheaper variant fails gate in staging or in the first X% of traffic, runtime automatically pulls route back to baseline; alerting and a minimal repro evaluation is kicked off.

Sample thresholds (proposal):
- Critical safety slice: pass >= 98.5% (binary safety checks)
- Instruction-following (top-level accuracy): delta <= 2.0 percentage points vs baseline
- Factuality (entity recall @ top-3): delta <= 3.5 percentage points
- Long-context coherency (>=1k tokens): delta <= 4.0 percentage points
- Latency degradation: p95 latency <= baseline p95 + 40ms
- Aggregate regression budget: weighted sum of deltas (weights by slice importance) <= 2.5 pts equivalence

How to translate regression budget to $ (Cost-of-Quality):
- Tie expected user impact to remediation costs. Example model used in spreadsheet:
  - Baseline: 0.2% user escalations / 1M requests (cost per escalation = $120)
  - Cheaper config might raise escalation rate by X. We convert X => expected additional escalations * cost per escalation = COQ.
  - Acceptable COQ for a given route = 0.02% * 1M * $120 = $240 (example)
- This lets product owners choose routes that can tolerate higher COQ (e.g., internal-only, low SLAs) vs those that cannot.

Spreadsheets and knobs (where/what to edit):
- Master cost model (linked): sheet "per-route-units" contains per-token cost, effective RPS buckets, and projected monthly savings for candidate variant at different traffic basis points (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%).
- Eval budget sheet: contains per-slice eval counts, per-eval compute cost, and human-review contingency budget.
- Gate config sheet: per-route gate thresholds, slice weights, and allowed COQ in dollars.
- Automation config: small JSON blob generated by the sheet (via Apps Script) that the deployment system ingests to know thresholds and enforcement actions.

Operational workflow (draft):
1) Product owner defines candidate variant & target routes in the sheet and selects slices.
2) Run automated eval suite in staging with identical traffic template (min sample size computed by the sheet). If passes gates -> move to canary.
3) Canary: route X% traffic to cheap variant with shadow logging of user satisfaction/metrics. Runtime enforces auto-fallback if any critical slice crosses emergency threshold.
4) After canary window (e.g., 48–72h) evaluate metrics and COQ; if under budget -> increase rollout. Repeat until target.

Rollout checklist (practical):
- [ ] Define slices for the route and set weights (required)
- [ ] Minimum sample size computed and scheduled in eval-suite (required)
- [ ] Update sheet with cost assumptions and projected savings (required)
- [ ] Create guardrail config entry (Apps Script export) (required)
- [ ] Canary window with shadow logging + baseline reruns (required)
- [ ] Post-canary slice-level signoff (owner + eng) (required)

Lightweight monitoring signals to compute during canary:
- slice pass-rates (automated unit tests)
- real-user feedback signal (thumbs, NPS proxy if available)
- error rates / hallucination detector scores
- latency p50/p95/p99 and tail CPU/GPU utilization

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Sample size vs cost: some rare-slice failures require very large samples to detect small regressions; we need a principled way to say "this route doesn't have enough signal, don't candidate it" or accept higher COQ.
- How to weight slices: currently manual; could we learn weights from historical incident costs?
- Partial pass semantics: do we allow a variant that beats baseline on most slices but slightly worse on a critical slice if COQ is small? (Recommendation: no for safety slices.)
- Cross-route shared models: if one model is rolled out across many routes, how to aggregate route-level COQ into a model-level allowance?

Immediate next steps (short term):
- Lina: update eval-sheet to add the weighted-budget calculator and Apps Script export (ETA 2w)
- Marco: prototype the runtime enforcement stub to read the guardrail JSON and auto-fallback (ETA 3w)
- Asha: run a sensitivity scan on 3 candidate variants for two internal routes and capture COQ vs savings curve (ETA 2w)
- Evan/Priya: define 6 canonical slices for platform teams and map existing eval tests to them (ETA 10d)

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- capture a couple of worked examples (internal chat assistant route; search-rewrite route) in the sheet.
- add short playbook text for SRE on how to respond to auto-fallback alerts (pager flow).
- keep the gating system opt-in per-org until we have more trust and historical signals.

Appendix: worked example (short):
- Route: internal-chat
- Baseline cost per 1M tokens: $420
- Cheap variant cost per 1M tokens: $310 -> savings $110 / 1M tokens (~26%)
- Measured aggregate delta in eval slices (weighted) = 1.1 pts -> allowed budget 2.5 -> PASS
- Projected monthly tokens for route = 20M => monthly savings ~$2.2k. Expected COQ (from spreadsheet) = $180. Net positive.

Endnotes / references:
- See linked spreadsheet for the exact formulas used to translate pass-rates to COQ.
- Related tickets: JIRA-OPT-1399 (quantized kernel perf regressions), JIRA-OPT-1407 (eval coverage gaps).

If you're reviewing: focused asks = (1) agree on the sample-size / cost guard that gates routes with low signal, (2) quick review of the sample weighted thresholds, (3) feedback on the rollback automation rules (aggressive vs conservative).
